title: AFL stars face lack of concussion coverage
full_text:
The AFL finals will proceed for the first time without a single player covered for concussion injuries following changes to their default protection that ended insurance coverage for head knocks.
The AFL Players Association has confirmed that no insurance company has offered to provide coverage for concussion under the footballers’ superannuation plan since financial services titan Zurich earlier this year declared that head trauma injuries were uninsurable. The cover expired on July 1.
This has left more than 500 players unable to make claims if they develop permanent brain injuries such as chronic traumatic encephalopathy, which can develop into dementia, as a result of suffering an on-field concussion.
Melbourne Football Club has since severed its sponsorship with Zurich at the end of the season after premiership star Angus Brayshaw was denied a seven-figure compensation claim. The irony is the Demons still carry the company’s logo on their jumpers. Demons forward Jacob van Rooyen’s high hit on Port Adelaide’s Aliir Aliir in Adelaide last Saturday concussed the defender.
The AFL has been engulfed in a concussion crisis after league commission chair Craig Drummond presided over a secret and unenforceable side deal when he was Geelong president that involved Cats player Jake Kolodjashnij signing away his legal rights.
The lack of insurance coverage has prompted calls for the AFL to establish an NFL-style fund to ensure players are financially protected if they sustain catastrophic head injuries.
Zurich had provided insurance under the AFL’s default superannuation plans, managed via AMP, for the past five years.
Ahead of the current agreement’s expiry, AMP asked other insurers to submit proposals to underwrite coverage. But none was offered.
Zurich was then asked to extend its terms. But when it ran its actuarial process and assessed the risk, it found concussion was uninsurable, namely because the link between concussion and development of permanent injuries such as CTE is unclear, though credibly argued. If an insurer cannot adequately assess a risk, it cannot price the risk, so it withdrew coverage.
Indeed, in the US, the NFL originally expected to pay out $US765m ($1.1bn) in claims under a proposed settlement in 2013. But a federal judge was concerned that the fund would run out of money and the league agreed to remove the cap. The fund has since paid out more than $US1.5bn, highlighting the severity of such injuries and difficulty in assessing the cost.
“There remains continued widespread uncertainty about the long-term health impacts and risks associated with concussion events from playing high contact sports, including the subsequent development of chronic traumatic encephalopathy,” a Zurich spokesman said.
“Beyond individual or group insurance arrangements, we acknowledge the establishment of the ‘Severe Injury Benefit’ by the AFL & AFLPA in May 2025, to support players who have suffered a significant cognitive or bodily impairment from playing football.” But the severe injury benefit scheme entitles payments of up to $600,000. This compares with the NFL’s concussion settlement paying out up to $US5m per player for the most severe diagnoses such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s and dementia.
CTE can also only be definitively diagnosed after death. St Kilda great and former Richmond coach Danny Frawley, Adelaide Crows AFLW player Heather Anderson, Geelong star Graham “Polly” Farmer and Richmond’s Shane Tuck were found to have CTE post-mortem.
The league’s AMP coverage has also been criticised over its ability to adequately cover players who are forced out of the game due to brain injuries, prompting players to take out their own premiums.
Kolodjashnij confirmed in 2024, the same year he signed the waiver at Geelong, that he had taken out additional cover. “It was a no-brainer to sort my own insurance cover out as the one we are under isn’t quite adequate,” Kolodjashnij said at the time.
Former Collingwood players Paul Seedsman and Nathan Murphy, who were both medically retired after concussion injuries, lost compensation payouts against Zurich in March, after the Australian Financial Complaints Authority sided with the insurance giant. The authority based its decision on the pair’s ability to perform basic daily activities – not their forced retirement from the AFL.
In May, former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw’s concussion claim was also rejected.
Still, AMP decided Zurich was the most appropriate insurance provider – even if it was the only provider that presented an insurance proposal.
“Zurich was requested to put forward a revised proposal for the provision of insurance within the AFLPA superannuation fund, the trustee for which is AMP,” a Zurich spokesman said.
“The trustee, in consultation with the AFLPA, determined Zurich’s proposal was the most appropriate when compared with other available market offerings.” Former AMP chief executive Alexis George, who retired from the wealth management firm in March, joined Zurich’s board last week as it deepens its push writing general and life insurance in the Australian market.
Kolodjashnij signed the waiver as a way for him to play after he received an inconclusive “amber” rating from the AFL’s concussion panel. Former Collingwood president Eddie McGuire said Kolodjashnij had played the last two seasons without a concussion, highlighting how the agreement extended his career.
But Mr McGuire criticised Geelong for not putting it in the official player contract, which required AFL sign-off. The AFL Players Association was in the dark about the side deal, with CEO James Gallagher saying “what happened at Geelong should never have occurred”.
A former league official has called for a fund to be established to tempt players into retirement if they receive more than three concussions, regardless of what the AFL’s concussion panel rules. Under the plan, a player would be paid a multiple of their current contracted earnings to retire.
